disprovenClaims: CLAIM (the phase's criterion 6): the server log will read 'opening ownership adopted: 2 of 5 capture point(s) start owned' because Island opens 0, 1, -1, -1, -1 and both sides start at multiplier x1. DISPROVEN by the run: the log reads '5 of 5', with points 1..4 all reported at 'scene owner 1'. And disproven for the OTHER map too, which is what makes it a claim about the code rather than about Island: 'grep -h "opening ownership adopted" artifacts/lane-b/*/server.log' returns '6 of 6' in 32 recorded Dustbowl runs. CapturePoint.Start's assaultMode branch calls SetOwner(1) on every owner:-1 point, SetOwner writes the owner field, and MatchController.Start reads GetOwner AFTER every CapturePoint.Start has run. Filed X-80.

CLAIM (the phase's section 3.2 field table): ServerMasterReporter._roomId 'is gone after P14 -- if P14 has not landed, leave the field at 0'. HALF DISPROVEN, and the half that matters is the source of the confusion: Dustbowl's YAML still literally contains '_roomId: 0', which is what the table was read from, but it is a DEAD KEY Unity has not rewritten. The clone re-serialized against the current class and dropped it. The field really is gone; the phase's evidence for its possible survival was stale serialization.

CLAIM (the phase's section 3.4): author 'a Level Bounds GameObject under the root Controllers'. DISPROVEN as stated: Island has fifteen roots and none of them is Controllers. A Controllers root was created to match Dustbowl's organisation; nothing under Assets/Scripts looks the name up (grep '"Controllers"' returns zero hits), so it is organisational only.

CLAIM (my own, held for most of the session): the client indexes capture points by an alphabetical FindObjectsOfType fallback while the server uses the authored array, so a deliberate _capturePoints order could desynchronise the flags. DISPROVEN by reading NetRoleBootstrap: it destroys nothing. Both bootstraps run in every process and each claims the role only if the other has not, so MatchController.Awake/Start runs on a client too and binds the SAME authored array. Only its repeating arithmetic is role-gated. The authored order is therefore consistent across both roles by construction -- and the run confirms it, with all three clients byte-identical on every point.

CLAIM (my own working assumption): the Windows player can be built from a live Editor via MCP. DISPROVEN by the Editor itself: EditorBuildWindowsHarness logs 'a live Editor cannot run this build: stripping UNITY_MCP_READY queues a script recompile, and BuildPlayer refuses to start during one' and names the batchmode path as the remedy. **The session memory was NOT wrong and this correction is the point:** it says in as many words that the player build refuses and the server build does not, and it even records that the EditorApplication.delayCall trick logs nothing at all for this method -- which is exactly what happened here, twice, before the message was read. The error was mine, in recalling a one-line summary instead of the note.
unverifiedClaims: A10's dangling-guid branch in GradeOne is not exercised by any mutation or fixture. Reaching it needs a prefab deleted out of the tree. Stated in gate-mutations.md rather than left for a reader to assume.

Criterion 2's 'from the menu' clause is not exercised by a click-path. The map-resolution code on that path was read and is entirely data-driven from MapCatalog, but nobody drove the P15/P16 screens against map 2 in this session.

The screenshots were watched, and what they show is stated: remote bodies, vehicles, a capture flag on its pole, the score bar at 208/8. They do NOT show two named players identifying each other, and they cannot show motion, which is why the position table from the checkpoints carries that half.

The one process error this session was mine and is recorded rather than smoothed over: the first mutation run restored Island.unity with 'git checkout --', which reverted the then-uncommitted authoring along with the mutation. It was caught on the next gate run (three findings reappeared naming map 2), the Editor still held the authored scene in memory, and the fix was to commit the authoring FIRST and redo the mutations against a file backup. Nothing was lost. The lesson is the standing one: commit before you mutate the thing you just built.
